analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA temporarily import foreign versions of drugs in shortage and speed up generic approval when too few companies make a drug.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee in March 2023 and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to temporarily allow importation of prescription drugs that are in shortage, as long as the drug is lifesaving or treats a debilitating condition, is already approved in certain foreign countries, and has the same active ingredient as the drug in short supply. It also would have let the FDA treat drugs with fewer than five approved makers and expired patents as being in a shortage even when they are not yet in one, triggering expedited generic review and importation. The goal was to end shortages of old, off-patent drugs where a small number of manufacturers face little competition. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who depend on drugs in shortage—especially lifesaving drugs like chemotherapy agents and injectable medicines that hospitals frequently cannot obtain—would get a reliable supply, since foreign-manufactured versions could be imported within 60 days of an application. People who pay high prices for old drugs where only a handful of companies make them would benefit from the competition the bill forces. Hospitals and pharmacies would spend less time scrambling for substitutes.

how_it_helps.text: It requires FDA to authorize temporary importation of prescription drugs that are lifesaving, life-sustaining, or treat debilitating conditions when those drugs are in shortage, with importation beginning within 60 days of a qualifying application and lasting up to three years or until the shortage ends.

It lets FDA treat drugs in 'marginally competitive' markets—where fewer than five approved versions are commercially available and patents have expired—as being in shortage, triggering expedited generic review and importation authority so a monopoly can be broken before it causes a shortage.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies that profit from shortages and from monopoly positions on old, off-patent drugs would face competition, lower prices, and the loss of shortage-driven price spikes. The FDA would bear the cost of reviewing and inspecting imported drugs.

drawbacks.text: FDA could deny an import request for safety or effectiveness reasons, and imported versions may carry labeling or quality differences that complicate use by U.S. providers, so the fix is not instant or risk-free.

The bill addresses symptoms rather than causes: shortages often stem from razor-thin generic drug pricing and few manufacturers, and temporary importation does not change the economics that make making old generic drugs unprofitable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—keeping lifesaving drugs in supply when a handful of manufacturers cannot—far outweighs the costs, which are modest: FDA must vet imported drugs for safety, and manufacturers lose the windfall profits shortages create. The main design weakness is that it treats symptoms (shortages in concentrated markets) rather than root causes like low generic reimbursement, but the cost of that limitation is small compared with the harm of empty pharmacy shelves.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 16, 2023 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken on it, and it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It carried bipartisan sponsorship from four senators, including two Republicans, yet never received a committee vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of old off-patent drugs keep the pricing power that comes from having few competitors, and patients remain exposed to shortages of essential medicines.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers with monopolies on old drugs

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan pair of co-sponsors.

for.name: Sens. Mike Lee, Dick Durbin, and Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill Republican as well as Democratic backing.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (industry opposition to importation generally)
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry has historically opposed drug importation measures on safety grounds; while no industry lobbying appears in the congressional record for this bill, the HELP Committee took no action on it.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no markup, no vote, no report—letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had four Senate sponsors split evenly between the parties (two Democrats, two Republicans), but the lack of any committee action means no votes were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers with monopoly positions on old off-patent drugs
industries.note: Importation and expedited generic approval undercut the quiet pricing power that comes from being one of a handful of suppliers of an old drug. Patients benefit when that monopoly is broken.
During a shortage, shortage-driven price spikes and exclusive supply contracts can be lucrative; temporary importation injects competition precisely when incumbent makers profit most from scarcity.
They would gain a more reliable drug supply but would bear the administrative work of sourcing and importing under new FDA authority.
